episodes.title: Is our national debt finally too much? (update)
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Planet Money revisits the US national debt debate, tracing it from the 2009 stimulus-era arguments through the influential (and later discredited) Reinhart-Rogoff "90% of GDP" threshold paper, and updates it with 2026 commentary from economists Karen Dynan and Kenneth Rogoff. The core shift: economists who once dismissed debt concerns are now turning hawkish as US Treasury yields have risen sharply, changing the calculus on debt sustainability for the world's benchmark risk-free asset.

**Key points**
- US gross national debt has crossed $40 trillion, up from ~$6-11 trillion in 2008-2012.
- The 2010 Reinhart-Rogoff paper claimed debt above 90% of GDP roughly halves growth; a 2013 spreadsheet error weakened but didn't overturn the correlation.
- Congress passed large tax cuts in 2025 that reduced revenue; debt service now exceeds $1 trillion/year, a record.
- The 10-year US Treasury yield recently hit its highest level since just before the Great Recession.
- CBO projects debt will cross 120% of GDP by 2036, higher than any prior point including WWII.
- Karen Dynan, a former dove, now calls herself a "debt hawk"; Kenneth Rogoff maintains his long-held hawkish stance and sees >50% odds of a significant debt-related shock.
- Both cite AI-driven investment buildout and geopolitical shocks (Iran war) as complicating factors for gauging debt tolerance.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising UST yields and deteriorating US fiscal trajectory are a global anchor: higher US term premia typically pressure DXY higher and tighten financial conditions, a headwind for EM carry trades and capital flows into EM Asia/LATAM.
- Persistent US fiscal deficits risk keeping US rates structurally higher, reducing the rate differential appeal of EM local-currency debt unless EM central banks maintain premium carry.
- A future US debt/rates shock (flagged by Rogoff/Dynan as a real tail risk) would likely trigger broad risk-off, hitting high-beta EM FX (BRL, COP, ZAR-like proxies, IDR) hardest.

**Watch list**
- US 10-year Treasury yield trajectory and any further spike toward pre-Great Recession highs.
- CBO debt/GDP projections (120% by 2036) versus actual fiscal trajectory under 2025 tax cuts.
- US interest expense as a share of budget (already >$1 trillion/year) — further increases could force fiscal adjustment (spending cuts/tax hikes) with knock-on effects for global rates and USD.

episodes.title: Yields Jump, A High-Stakes Visit, and Lefrak’s Real Estate Warning 9/23/26
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A sharp, PMI-driven Treasury sell-off dominates the session — the 10-year yield broke above 5% to a 19-year high and the 2-year jumped 18bp — alongside a hawkish repricing of Fed hike odds and a weak 5-year auction, just as President Xi arrives in Washington for a high-stakes state visit with Trump. The move is global in scope (UST, JGB, French OATs all selling off) and directly repriced Fed policy expectations, dollar strength and risk appetite — all first-order channels into EM FX and rates.

**Key points**
- 10-year UST yield hit 5.09-5.10%, highest in 19 years; 2-year near 4.94-4.95%, up 13-18bp on the day.
- October rate-hike probability jumped to 64% from 55% a day earlier and just 8% a month ago; markets pricing nearly 4 more hikes into 2027.
- Flash S&P PMI composite jumped to 58.4, highest since July 2021, with severe supply-chain bottlenecks and accelerating input-cost inflation.
- 5-year note auction tailed 3.3bp, worst since June 2006, with weak dealer/indirect demand; Santelli flagged 5.17-5.21% as next resistance on the 10-year.
- Diesel at a record $6.52/gallon is cited as the key inflation driver (more than crude); White House reportedly considering a 90-day ban on diesel exports, which knocked diesel futures down as much as 6%.
- DXY near a two-month high on hawkish Fed repricing; gold turned negative for the month; WTI ~$92, up ~1%.
- Xi-Trump summit: no major breakthroughs expected; possible deliverables include extending the Busan trade truce, an AI safety dialogue, more Chinese ag/aircraft purchases; Taiwan arms package ($14bn) remains stalled; rare earths leverage over the US persists.
- China tech (KWEB) down sharply YTD (Alibaba -24%, Tencent -53%, Baidu -31%) versus AI hardware/semis (KraneShares KSTAR) outperforming by ~60pp; guest flagged possible removal of $30bn reciprocal tariffs and a US-China trade commission as constructive scenarios.

**FX / rates implications**
- Sharply higher UST yields and a stronger DXY are a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades broadly — higher core yields compress EM rate differentials and typically pressure INR, IDR, PHP, MXN, BRL, COP via the standard risk-off/UST channel.
- A hawkish Fed repricing (October hike odds at 64%) raises the bar for EM central banks (RBI, BI, BSP, Banxico, BCB) to ease, and argues for continued vigilance on FX intervention/fixings in high-beta EM currencies.
- Diesel/oil-driven inflation and a possible US export ban on diesel could tighten global diesel supply, an upside risk to energy-import-dependent EM current accounts.
- Extension of the Busan trade truce or tariff rollback from the Xi-Trump summit would be a modest risk-on catalyst for CNY, and by extension the broader EM Asia FX complex (KRW, TWD, MYR) given China trade linkages.

**Watch list**
- Xi-Trump summit outcomes this week: Busan trade truce extension, tariff/rare-earths signals, Taiwan arms package decision.
- 10-year UST resistance levels flagged at 5.17-5.19% and 5.21%; next FOMC meeting in October (64% hike probability).
- White House diesel export ban decision (90-day proposal) and diesel price trajectory off the $6.52 record.
- Upcoming official ISM manufacturing report versus today's flash PMI beat.

episodes.title: The 5% yield
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
The 10-year US Treasury yield touched 5% this week before easing back below that level, a psychologically significant threshold given the benchmark's role pricing US mortgages, corporate debt, and global borrowing costs. For an EM trader, the move matters less as a standalone shock and more as a signal of where US real rates, term premium, and risk appetite are heading into year-end.

**Key points**
- 10-year UST yield hit roughly 4.96-5% before pulling back under 5%, up a full percentage point since late February when US/Israel airstrikes on Iran began, versus below 4% before that.
- Fed Chair (referred to as Kevin Warsh in transcript) attributed the rise in long yields to US economic strength, competition for capital from AI-driven corporate debt issuance (data center buildout), and geopolitics/wars.
- US total debt is $40tn, with $32tn in Treasuries (up from under $20tn pre-COVID); annual deficit is 5.7% of GDP; interest expense on debt now exceeds $1tn/year (~$1.2tn this year), the second-largest budget category after entitlements.
- Unlike the volatile 2023 run to 5% (tied to Fed hiking amid 9% CPI), this move has been slower and more orderly, with no sign of bid-ask spread widening or market dislocation; investment-grade and even junk credit spreads remain tight/narrowing.
- US consumer spending (strong retail sales, core/control-group up most in ~2 years) remains resilient, skewed toward top earners; Atlanta Fed GDPNow tracking above 5% for Q3, consensus above 3%.
- Treasury Secretary Bessent's attempt to talk/buy back yields lower has so far failed to bring 10-year yields down meaningfully.

**FX / rates implications**
- Elevated UST yields keep the dollar underpinned via rate differentials, a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades (INR, IDR, PHP, MXN, BRL) if yields resume climbing toward 5%+.
- Rising US term premium and fiscal/debt sustainability concerns (debt-to-GDP ~100%+, deficit 5.7% of GDP) could keep global long-end yields elevated (mentioned spillover to European yields too), pressuring EM local-currency bond valuations and steepening EM curves in sympathy.
- Credit spreads (IG and junk) remaining tight signals no near-term risk-off stress for EM external debt or high-yield sovereigns despite higher UST yields.
- Geopolitical/oil-driven inflation risk (Iran conflict) is a channel worth monitoring for EM oil importers (India, Philippines, Thailand) via energy price pass-through.

**Watch list**
- US midterm elections (~one month out) and any fiscal policy shifts affecting Treasury issuance/deficit trajectory.
- Further Fed commentary on inflation persistence and balance-sheet/issuance dynamics.
- Whether 10-year yield revisits 5% and how orderly (bid-ask spreads) that move is versus 2023's volatility.
